full_text:
Interviewer:	I’ll start off telling you a bit about what we’re doing. We’re interviewing women engineers from all the different disciplines and finding out things like why they decided to do engineering, some of their experiences in going to university and the course so far. And then – are you going on the placement?

Subject:	Yeah

Interviewer:	Ok and then how you decided to go on the placement and what you expect to get out of it, and then going on to what you hope to do career wise – anything like that (OK). What we’re hoping to do is understand women’s first encounters with the engineering industry and hopefully improve the situation, for women, in engineering. So at the end of the project, which is a 2 year project, we’re going to put together a guidance document to give to the Engineering Council and hopefully improve the situation for women in engineering. If it’s Ok with you, I’ll just start by asking you a few background questions and then move on to ask about the course and things like that. Is it chemical engineering that you’re doing?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	Are you doing a masters or …?

Subject:	No I’m doing the bachelors.

Interviewer:	OK did you do A levels?

Subject:	No, I did foundation in [town], yeah (OK) It was only for 8 months.

Interviewer:	Did you do that at a different university, did you say?

Subject:	In [town]. One of the colleges in [town].

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

Subject:	I went to a convent school in [Country] – yeah, for primary and high school. Then 

Interviewer:	Was it a girls’ school?

Subject:	Yeah. An all girls school. Then I came over to Bath to do my foundation. After GCSE in [country]. Then I did that for 8 months and then I like did my first year here.

Interviewer:	Ok, have you got any previous work experience in the industry?

Subject:	Erm, I haven’t no.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. What about your parents, what do they do? Are either of them engineers at all?

Subject:	Er no, my father is a business man and my mother is a housewife.

Interviewer:	OK So when and why then do you think that you decided to do engineering?

Subject:	Er, it was when I was in [town]. I was doing in the Foundation year and I had like when I was – about to apply for university, I have to choose what er course I have to do. I chose, ‘cos erm I studied science all the while, so I actually wanted to choose pharmacy ‘cos I quite like chemistry, but then er because I didn’t do A’’ levels, so most of the universities they didn’t accept foundation. So I applied for chemical engineering and that’s because of – it has a wider er band of opportunities – work opportunities.

Interviewer:	OK, was the foundation course in a particular subject?

Subject:	Erm, yeah erm it was I think chemistry, physics, mathematics and (further?)

Interviewer:	OK have your family been supportive of you wanting to do engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, they don’t mind what course I choose as long as I enjoy doing it.

Interviewer:	Did you have any careers advice at all?

Subject:	Not really no.

Interviewer:	OK when you decided to do engineering, did you do any career research to see what sort of opportunities there would be at the end of it or anything like that?

Subject:	Yeah, I found that most of the chemical engineers look for oil companies like er [company] or [company] but then I’m not sure what they actually do. They do it on my course.

Interviewer:	OK What do you think it is that appeals to you about chemical engineering?

Subject:	I’m not sure ‘cos what I thought like most – like most other women I think I think engineering now only for men. Yeah, like when I joined the women engineering society – like we need to influence the young girls – high school girls and tell them about engineering. I was like one of those type of girls – I didn’t know anything.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the reason that more women don’t do engineering is because they don’t know what it is in the first place?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah, I think so, ‘cos most of the engineering, they’re all about designing work, designing like – just different parts of design and just – I think it’s studying engineering is like studying all other subjects – all other course. Not much different.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this] University?

Subject:	Because I’ve chosen chemical engineering – er, I have one of friends that studied here and she did chemical engineering as well and she said that this university’s quite good for chemical engineering and I found out from the Times and I saw the rating was quite high, for chemical engineering. Also it is was the placement and that was one of the main reason I chose this university.

Interviewer:	Yeah, because of the placement?

Subject:	Yeah – the placement.

Interviewer:	Did you always know that you wanted to do a placement?

Subject:	Yeah, because my – because my family – it’ll be like – it will lighten the burden of my family because they have to pay overseas fees.

Interviewer:	OK. When you started engineering, did you realise it was so male dominated?

Subject:	When I started at the university here? I found – my course, I found er quite er quite much number of women engineers.

Interviewer:	Yeah, was it more than you expected it to be?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	How many women are there on your course?

Subject:	I think there are more than 10 women. And there is something like 14 on our course.

Interviewer:	OK, OK. Did it ever bother you that there weren’t that many women?

Subject:	No, not really.

Interviewer:	Ok, what characteristics do you think make a good engineer?

Subject:	They have to be quite careful, careful with all the calculations. If they go wrong then everything will be wrong. And then just try to be organised and you have to sort out what you’re supposed to do first and then just plan everything before which needs doing.

Interviewer:	Do you think that any of those characteristics are more male or female characteristics?

Subject:	I think both will have those characteristics. It depends on those people who…

Interviewer:	OK, Do you think there are any advantages or disadvantages to being a woman engineer?

Subject:	Hmm, I think the disadvantages will be like maybe the companies employing people will – might prefer to employ a male engineer. I’m not sure. Maybe er like, maybe they meet – they think that male engineers are better.

Interviewer:	Do you think that there are any advantages?

Subject:	Mm, I don’t know – maybe some people might think that women engineers are more careful than men.

Interviewer:	Let’s talk a bit about the course now. Has the degree, so far, been what you expected it to be?

Subject:	Mm, it was quite a tough course, yeah, but I think that if I – if I work extra, like work harder on it, it should be OK, yeah. Besides (?) I work part-time as well. Yeah.

Interviewer:	What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course?

Subject:	Er, best thing is my – all my course mates so they’re really friendly and they’re really helpful, not like some other course. ‘Cos I visit – my course is just small group of people. Some other courses they – like they don’t know who are on the course, and they don’t communicate. In my course it’s quite good. And then we have some design course work where we have to work in groups and we have 4 different course works and we changed our groups each time, so we get to know other people on the course, so yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, when you work in groups, do you choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

Subject:	No, we get put into groups but then we have er the laboratory where we can choose.

Interviewer:	OK, how do you decide who you’re going to work with when you get to choose?

Subject:	When I get to choose, I just choose someone next to me actually. That’s actually in the form it comes along, so I just fill in my name and the next person and my friend is sitting next to me, so but his name down.

Interviewer:	Do you prefer to work with other women, or men, or don’t you mind?

Subject:	I don’t really mind, as long as he is to – he or she will contribute like to what we’re doing.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Subject:	Erm, I think most of the women in my class are more hard working, probably because they feel that they’re not – as good as the men maybe, I don’t know, but then like most of them are hard working so I prefer to work with the woman maybe.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s fine. Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

Subject:	Yeah, I’ve had a – one male partner last year, in my first year. Er I didn’t choose him, the problem is I was put into that group – just me and him doing like work. He – every time he didn’t turn up for lectures or even come to meet me for the meetings and he just go and play games and all that. And then I just have to do everything alone. I talked to my personal tutor about it and he say he will sort it out for me.

Interviewer:	Did he help then?

Subject:	I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think in that situation it would have been different if you were working with a woman or do you think it was just that particular male?

Subject:	I think it’s just that person.

Interviewer:	OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	None?

Subject:	No

Interviewer:	So would you have liked to be taught by some female lecturers?

Subject:	Yeah, it will be different. Maybe show some different methods of teaching that will be more efficient.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is encouraging as well? Sort of if they can do, I can do it?

Subject:	Y - what, sorry?

Interviewer:	Do you think it would be encouraging having female lecturers because you might think if they can do it, I can do it as well?

Subject:	Yeah – probably – yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

Subject:	Mm, some – I think most of them treat us the same but sometimes maybe you can see that they are treating the male engineers betters. But maybe because they are bolder. When in the class they answer the questions and that’s why and everything. That maybe.

Interviewer:	You said you’ve got a personal tutor, are they male?

Subject:	Yeah, male.

Interviewer:	Do you find that they’re quite approachable or would you like a…?

Subject:	Er, my personal tutor, he’s quite nice. Yeah he’s – he always welcomes us for questions and he always helps us.

Interviewer:	OK, and you wouldn’t rather have a female personal tutor?

Subject:	I don’t mind.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that any parts of the teaching, or advice that you’ve had, will help you when you go on your placement?

Subject:	Er, yeah, I think most of them will help.

Interviewer:	Do you think it is mainly technical skills that you’re going to take into the placement, or have you learnt anything else as well?

Subject:	Well our course is set in the way that you – it will help us when we go into work and industry, so I don’t think there will be a problem for me to go out into industry yeah. And most of the – I think for the technical part and the period like the – that they are quite well taught.

Interviewer:	Do you think you’ve learnt anything else like … do you think the group work that you’ve done, do you think that will help you when you go into the industry?

Subject:	I think it will help because I think when you go in industry, I need to work with different people so this – it’s trying to communicate with people and I think that’s the skill that I’m getting from the design coursework.

Interviewer:	OK, do you feel like you’re ready and prepared to go on placement now?

Subject:	Hmm, I’m not sure. I don’t think so because I don’t know what I will be – I know what I’ll be doing – I’ll be doing like emissions from the gases of the exhausts of the cars. I will be testing those emissions but I’m not sure what skills I’ll need. I know I’ll need to show computer skills like doing an excel spread sheet but apart from that I’m not sure.

Interviewer:	OK, have you spoken to any students that have been on placement already?

Subject:	Er, there are – when you were about to apply for placement er my – one of my lecturers actually arranged for us to meet someone come back from placement, to give us a talk – yeah.

Interviewer:	Has that helped at all?

Subject:	Er it was quite – they were just talking about a few companies and where you will be based and how we should go about getting accommodation, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the educational experience and the way that you’re taught will reflect what it’s like when you’re in the industry or do you think that will be a totally different situation?

Subject:	I feel it will be different – it will be quite different. It just – I think when I go on placement, I don’t need that much – because my placement didn’t say that I have to know all what’s in my course and everything. It just say I need to like – know what you’re doing, know the – like my title, what I am supposed to do and then I’ll be fine. And there will be people there to help me, so…it will be alright.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you will get treated differently being at work, to being at university?

Subject:	Maybe – I hope not.

Interviewer:	What do you hope might be different?

Subject:	I just – it’s – I mean, I don’t (if there will be someone I can go to and ask questions?) but I will have this supervisor who will just help me, like if I need her.

Interviewer:	OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on the placement?

Subject:	To go on (?) Because I’ve been to many interviews but I didn’t get any of the place. And this one I’ve been in, I just got it and I – I went to the company, didn’t (?) the interview and I saw that it’s quite good – it’s quite a good company – it’s [company]? (yes) It’s quite a big company and they’re offering like the job they’ll be doing, it’s quite good. And I’ve met the supervisors that I will be working with and they’re quite nice, so I think it’s OK.

Interviewer:	OK, did you look at anything else like location or training opportunities or whether you could get a job at the end of it, or anything like that?

Subject:	Er, I don’t mind the location because er it’s quite good, it’s in [town]. Yeah, er I don’t mind really if it’s not in [town] but er like I work – because the work that they’re giving me is not, maybe er involved a lot of chemical engineering work like I don’t get to work in the refinery – I will just need to book computer days work but I prefer to have accommodation on board or maybe some more connection with my class but then I’m worried that if I don’t accept that offer then I may not get a placement at all, in the end. So – I talked to my supervisor that I prefer to work er for like not just computer based or if they want to give me any lab work, I don’t mind at all and she say she’ll try to arrange it.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the benefits of going on the placement then?

Subject:	Er, I think there are quite a few benefits. I think we can get work experience. I really working as an engineer yeah, but like the part-time jobs. And then, get to meet more people and then some extra money.

Interviewer:	Do you think it will help you get a job when you finish university?

Subject:	Yeah, I think – I think that – because I saw the web site, most of the web sites mention that if we get a placement it will be like er like er an advance stage to the graduate recruitment. So it’s quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, was the internet your main source of finding out about the different companies or did you use any other ways of finding out about companies?

Subject:	Yeah, I used the internet most of the time, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, did the university help much in finding you a placement?

Subject:	Yeah. My department is quite good because I think my department, compared to all other faculties that I could – my department will help us to apply for placement. They took our CV’s and send it out to companies – we just had to write our names in the bottom – which companies we wanted interview with – yeah. That’s how we all get the placement and that. We don’t have to apply ourselves.

Interviewer:	OK, would you like the university to do anything else to help you, or do you think they did everything that they could?

Subject:	Er, it’s quite good and we’ve got a lecturer – er we have one module – like separated in one small part for the industrial placement and he taught us about the interviews and thing.

Interviewer:	That’s good.

Subject:	He invited the people from careers service to give us talk about our placement – quite good.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think will be the best things and the worst things about being on placement?

Subject:	The best thing is I am get –er what I hope for, like the experiences and er meeting people, making friends. The worst thing er maybe there’s some problems that I can’t solve if you’re in the placement or maybe meet some people who are not like friendly.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s it I think about that. In terms of your career then, what do you think that you’ll be doing in say 5 years time?

Subject:	I hope to be in chemical engineering (yeah). I hope to work er and going back to [country].

Interviewer:	You’d like to work in this country first?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what about in say 10 years time? Would you like to go into management?

Subject:	Yeah, I – I er actually at first I thought I would – I’ve been picking (?) chemical engineers because I want to do masters in business studies – business course. Then, hmm like I am not sure if I can do it all. Maybe I get some work experience first before I start the masters course – yeah. I would like to do a different masters course from engineering – engineering.

Interviewer:	But you’d like a job in engineering to begin with?

Subject:	Yeah, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that when you go into the management or business side – do you think that will be managing other engineers then?

Subject:	Yeah – I, yeah. But not totally like business.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. What do you think would be your ideal job then?

Subject:	Mm, ideal job er I’m not too sure – chemical engineering, yeah.

Interviewer:	Is it specific part of …?

Subject:	Yeah, chemical engineer.

Interviewer:	Do you want to get your Chartership?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’ll have any difficulties, trying to get the chartership at all?

Subject:	Mm, I – I’m not sure but it should be – it shouldn’t be too hard because the IChemE they came to give us a presentation, at the start of last year, and they say I will just need work experiences and I had to join IChemE to get chartership and they will like tell us how to do it when we – really like want to do it.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in chemical engineering?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so because it has diverse working opportunities. Because we can work in like pharmaceuticals oil companies or both, there are lots of different companies where we can work for. Yeah, and all the (products that we make?) are like for the (dailies?) yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, which bit of chemical engineering do you think you’d like to go into and…?

Subject:	At first, because I like from – I would like to study pharmaceuticals so I thought I would like to work in pharmaceuticals company, but then I asked some agents in Malaysia – they say that pharmaceuticals they’re not very er wide in Malaysia. But I mean like one company in all Malaysia that does pharmaceuticals so they say I should just try to work in any companies and not just choose pharmaceuticals. I try to think of these – it’s OK because I can get different experiences (?) yeah.

Interviewer:	Is engineering as male dominated in [country] as it is in Britain?

Subject:	I think yes – no, I think it’s the same. But – yeah because I have like my – er my class in Malaysia – I was in an all girls school, yeah, and like the whole class they would all like to er be engineers.

Interviewer:	Really?

Subject:	Yeah.

Interviewer:	That’s very different from here. Do you think that was because you were at a girls school?

Subject:	Maybe because I was in a science class because all the sciences were – most of them wanted to be engineers

Interviewer:	Did you have more information in [country] about what engineering was?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? If you went through it all again would you do anything differently?

Subject:	Mm, you mean as when I choose my course?

Interviewer:	Yeah.

Subject:	If I did ‘A’ levels, I might apply for pharmacy but then pharmacy – if I did pharmacy, I didn’t get to do placement because I didn’t think they have placement on pharmacy and I would have to do a masters course in pharmacy, because it’s a 4 year master course. So there might be disadvantages so mm I think I will still choose engineering and so…

Interviewer:	Have you enjoyed this course?

Subject:	Yeah, it’s erm – it’s quite – I think it’s not that hard it’s just that I need to put extra time on it.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the chemical engineering industry?

Subject:	Er, fun? Interesting, er stressed – with all the calculations, erm organised and designed.

Interviewer:	OK, would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

Subject:	Sorry?

Interviewer:	Would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

Subject:	No.

Interviewer:	No? why do you think that engineering is so male dominated?

Subject:	Erm, I don’t know, probably some – most of the things that they’re – most female maybe they think they will do something like business or engineering not suitable for them or er some of those do like fashion designing – females there’s a lot more and for males and they’re all like – they’re first jobs they’re definitely – like, from what I think they would not choose like fashion design and things like that. So maybe engineering is…

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s all to do with how boys and girls are brought up as children?

Subject:	Yeah, I think so.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the fact that there are so many males in the industry will ever cause you any problems at all?

Subject:	I think there won’t be any problems. I think there should be – it should be quite helpful and now many, many women are equal.

Interviewer:	That’s OK. That’s good. That’s everything – thank you very much. Thank you for your help.

turns.text: Do you think that there are any advantages?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I don’t know – maybe some people might think that women engineers are more careful than men.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Let’s talk a bit about the course now. Has the degree, so far, been what you expected it to be?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, it was quite a tough course, yeah, but I think that if I – if I work extra, like work harder on it, it should be OK, yeah. Besides (?) I work part-time as well. Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, best thing is my – all my course mates so they’re really friendly and they’re really helpful, not like some other course. ‘Cos I visit – my course is just small group of people. Some other courses they – like they don’t know who are on the course, and they don’t communicate. In my course it’s quite good. And then we have some design course work where we have to work in groups and we have 4 different course works and we changed our groups each time, so we get to know other people on the course, so yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, when you work in groups, do you choose who you want to work with or do you get put into groups?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No, we get put into groups but then we have er the laboratory where we can choose.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, how do you decide who you’re going to work with when you get to choose?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: When I get to choose, I just choose someone next to me actually. That’s actually in the form it comes along, so I just fill in my name and the next person and my friend is sitting next to me, so but his name down.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you prefer to work with other women, or men, or don’t you mind?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t really mind, as long as he is to – he or she will contribute like to what we’re doing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I think most of the women in my class are more hard working, probably because they feel that they’re not – as good as the men maybe, I don’t know, but then like most of them are hard working so I prefer to work with the woman maybe.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s fine. Have you had any particularly bad experiences of group work?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I’ve had a – one male partner last year, in my first year. Er I didn’t choose him, the problem is I was put into that group – just me and him doing like work. He – every time he didn’t turn up for lectures or even come to meet me for the meetings and he just go and play games and all that. And then I just have to do everything alone. I talked to my personal tutor about it and he say he will sort it out for me.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did he help then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think in that situation it would have been different if you were working with a woman or do you think it was just that particular male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it’s just that person.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you been taught by any female lecturers at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: None?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: So would you have liked to be taught by some female lecturers?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it will be different. Maybe show some different methods of teaching that will be more efficient.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is encouraging as well? Sort of if they can do, I can do it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Y - what, sorry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it would be encouraging having female lecturers because you might think if they can do it, I can do it as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – probably – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the lecturers treat the male and female students the same?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, some – I think most of them treat us the same but sometimes maybe you can see that they are treating the male engineers betters. But maybe because they are bolder. When in the class they answer the questions and that’s why and everything. That maybe.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You said you’ve got a personal tutor, are they male?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, male.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you find that they’re quite approachable or would you like a…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, my personal tutor, he’s quite nice. Yeah he’s – he always welcomes us for questions and he always helps us.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, and you wouldn’t rather have a female personal tutor?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I don’t mind.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that any parts of the teaching, or advice that you’ve had, will help you when you go on your placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, yeah, I think most of them will help.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it is mainly technical skills that you’re going to take into the placement, or have you learnt anything else as well?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Well our course is set in the way that you – it will help us when we go into work and industry, so I don’t think there will be a problem for me to go out into industry yeah. And most of the – I think for the technical part and the period like the – that they are quite well taught.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think you’ve learnt anything else like … do you think the group work that you’ve done, do you think that will help you when you go into the industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think it will help because I think when you go in industry, I need to work with different people so this – it’s trying to communicate with people and I think that’s the skill that I’m getting from the design coursework.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you feel like you’re ready and prepared to go on placement now?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Hmm, I’m not sure. I don’t think so because I don’t know what I will be – I know what I’ll be doing – I’ll be doing like emissions from the gases of the exhausts of the cars. I will be testing those emissions but I’m not sure what skills I’ll need. I know I’ll need to show computer skills like doing an excel spread sheet but apart from that I’m not sure.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, have you spoken to any students that have been on placement already?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, there are – when you were about to apply for placement er my – one of my lecturers actually arranged for us to meet someone come back from placement, to give us a talk – yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Has that helped at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er it was quite – they were just talking about a few companies and where you will be based and how we should go about getting accommodation, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that the educational experience and the way that you’re taught will reflect what it’s like when you’re in the industry or do you think that will be a totally different situation?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I feel it will be different – it will be quite different. It just – I think when I go on placement, I don’t need that much – because my placement didn’t say that I have to know all what’s in my course and everything. It just say I need to like – know what you’re doing, know the – like my title, what I am supposed to do and then I’ll be fine. And there will be people there to help me, so…it will be alright.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you will get treated differently being at work, to being at university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe – I hope not.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: What do you hope might be different?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I just – it’s – I mean, I don’t (if there will be someone I can go to and ask questions?) but I will have this supervisor who will just help me, like if I need her.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, why did you decide that you wanted to go on the placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: To go on (?) Because I’ve been to many interviews but I didn’t get any of the place. And this one I’ve been in, I just got it and I – I went to the company, didn’t (?) the interview and I saw that it’s quite good – it’s quite a good company – it’s [company]? (yes) It’s quite a big company and they’re offering like the job they’ll be doing, it’s quite good. And I’ve met the supervisors that I will be working with and they’re quite nice, so I think it’s OK.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did you look at anything else like location or training opportunities or whether you could get a job at the end of it, or anything like that?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I don’t mind the location because er it’s quite good, it’s in [town]. Yeah, er I don’t mind really if it’s not in [town] but er like I work – because the work that they’re giving me is not, maybe er involved a lot of chemical engineering work like I don’t get to work in the refinery – I will just need to book computer days work but I prefer to have accommodation on board or maybe some more connection with my class but then I’m worried that if I don’t accept that offer then I may not get a placement at all, in the end. So – I talked to my supervisor that I prefer to work er for like not just computer based or if they want to give me any lab work, I don’t mind at all and she say she’ll try to arrange it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the benefits of going on the placement then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, I think there are quite a few benefits. I think we can get work experience. I really working as an engineer yeah, but like the part-time jobs. And then, get to meet more people and then some extra money.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think it will help you get a job when you finish university?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think – I think that – because I saw the web site, most of the web sites mention that if we get a placement it will be like er like er an advance stage to the graduate recruitment. So it’s quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, was the internet your main source of finding out about the different companies or did you use any other ways of finding out about companies?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I used the internet most of the time, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, did the university help much in finding you a placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah. My department is quite good because I think my department, compared to all other faculties that I could – my department will help us to apply for placement. They took our CV’s and send it out to companies – we just had to write our names in the bottom – which companies we wanted interview with – yeah. That’s how we all get the placement and that. We don’t have to apply ourselves.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you like the university to do anything else to help you, or do you think they did everything that they could?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, it’s quite good and we’ve got a lecturer – er we have one module – like separated in one small part for the industrial placement and he taught us about the interviews and thing.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s good.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: He invited the people from careers service to give us talk about our placement – quite good.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what do you think will be the best things and the worst things about being on placement?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: The best thing is I am get –er what I hope for, like the experiences and er meeting people, making friends. The worst thing er maybe there’s some problems that I can’t solve if you’re in the placement or maybe meet some people who are not like friendly.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, that’s it I think about that. In terms of your career then, what do you think that you’ll be doing in say 5 years time?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I hope to be in chemical engineering (yeah). I hope to work er and going back to [country].

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: You’d like to work in this country first?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what about in say 10 years time? Would you like to go into management?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I – I er actually at first I thought I would – I’ve been picking (?) chemical engineers because I want to do masters in business studies – business course. Then, hmm like I am not sure if I can do it all. Maybe I get some work experience first before I start the masters course – yeah. I would like to do a different masters course from engineering – engineering.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: But you’d like a job in engineering to begin with?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Do you think that when you go into the management or business side – do you think that will be managing other engineers then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah – I, yeah. But not totally like business.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah, OK. What do you think would be your ideal job then?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, ideal job er I’m not too sure – chemical engineering, yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is it specific part of …?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, chemical engineer.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you want to get your Chartership?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that you’ll have any difficulties, trying to get the chartership at all?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, I – I’m not sure but it should be – it shouldn’t be too hard because the IChemE they came to give us a presentation, at the start of last year, and they say I will just need work experiences and I had to join IChemE to get chartership and they will like tell us how to do it when we – really like want to do it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in chemical engineering?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so because it has diverse working opportunities. Because we can work in like pharmaceuticals oil companies or both, there are lots of different companies where we can work for. Yeah, and all the (products that we make?) are like for the (dailies?) yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, which bit of chemical engineering do you think you’d like to go into and…?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: At first, because I like from – I would like to study pharmaceuticals so I thought I would like to work in pharmaceuticals company, but then I asked some agents in Malaysia – they say that pharmaceuticals they’re not very er wide in Malaysia. But I mean like one company in all Malaysia that does pharmaceuticals so they say I should just try to work in any companies and not just choose pharmaceuticals. I try to think of these – it’s OK because I can get different experiences (?) yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Is engineering as male dominated in [country] as it is in Britain?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: I think yes – no, I think it’s the same. But – yeah because I have like my – er my class in Malaysia – I was in an all girls school, yeah, and like the whole class they would all like to er be engineers.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Really?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: That’s very different from here. Do you think that was because you were at a girls school?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Maybe because I was in a science class because all the sciences were – most of them wanted to be engineers

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Did you have more information in [country] about what engineering was?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK. Are you happy with all the career choices that you’ve made so far? If you went through it all again would you do anything differently?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Mm, you mean as when I choose my course?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: If I did ‘A’ levels, I might apply for pharmacy but then pharmacy – if I did pharmacy, I didn’t get to do placement because I didn’t think they have placement on pharmacy and I would have to do a masters course in pharmacy, because it’s a 4 year master course. So there might be disadvantages so mm I think I will still choose engineering and so…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Have you enjoyed this course?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, it’s erm – it’s quite – I think it’s not that hard it’s just that I need to put extra time on it.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the chemical engineering industry?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Er, fun? Interesting, er stressed – with all the calculations, erm organised and designed.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: OK, would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Sorry?

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Would you use masculine as a word to describe it?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: No.

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: No? why do you think that engineering is so male dominated?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Erm, I don’t know, probably some – most of the things that they’re – most female maybe they think they will do something like business or engineering not suitable for them or er some of those do like fashion designing – females there’s a lot more and for males and they’re all like – they’re first jobs they’re definitely – like, from what I think they would not choose like fashion design and things like that. So maybe engineering is…

turns.speaker: Interviewer
turns.text: Do you think that’s all to do with how boys and girls are brought up as children?

turns.speaker: Subject
turns.text: Yeah, I think so.

turns.text: OK, do you think that the fact that there are so many males in the industry will ever cause you any problems at all?
